claim: The lagging X chromosome in C. elegans males during anaphase I is due to lack of chromosome pairing.
source: Using live imaging and tomographic reconstructions of spermatocyte meiotic spindles in Caenorhabditis elegans, we find the lagging X chromosome, a distinctive feature of anaphase I in C. elegans males, is due to lack of chromosome pairing.
evidence: The manuscript presents live imaging and tomographic data showing that unpaired chromosomes lag during anaphase I.

claim: The unpaired X chromosome remains tethered to centrosomes by lengthening kinetochore microtubules during anaphase I.
source: The unpaired chromosome remains tethered to centrosomes by lengthening kinetochore microtubules, which are under tension, suggesting that a 'tug of war' reliably resolves lagging.

claim: Kinetochore microtubules attached to the lagging X chromosome are under tension.

source: As in many other species, C. elegans centrosomes are present in spermatocyte meiosis (Wolf et al., 1978) and embryonic mitosis (O'Toole et al., 2003) but not in oocyte meiosis, where inter-chromosomal microtubules are reported to push chromosomes apart (Dumont et al., 2010; Laband et al., 2017; Redemann et al., 2018; Yu et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

source: Meiotic kinetochore structure and dynamics, however, vary from mitosis, where kinetochores attach each sister to microtubules from opposite poles during the single division.

source: Meiotic kinetochores must detach and re-attach to microtubules to allow sisters to switch from segregating to the same pole in meiosis I to opposite poles in meiosis II (Petronczki et al., 2003).

source: For example, during the first centrosomal mitotic division in C. elegans, pole-to-pole separation (anaphase B) but not chromosome-to-pole shortening (anaphase A) drives chromosome movement (Nahaboo et al., 2015; Oegema et al., 2001; Scholey et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

source: In C. elegans acentrosomal oocyte spindles, shortening of the distance between chromosomes and poles was observed before microtubules disassemble at the acentrosomal poles (McNally et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Spermatocyte chromosomes arrange in a rosette pattern, with paired autosomes surrounding the unpaired X chromosome in metaphase I.
source: Spermatocyte chromosomes arrange in a rosette pattern, with paired autosomes surrounding the unpaired X chromosome in metaphase I (Albertson and Thomson, 1993).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature and confirmed by the live imaging data in the manuscript.

claim: In anaphase I, homologs segregate towards opposite poles while the unpaired X chromosome remains behind and attached to microtubules connected to separating poles before resolving to one side.
source: In anaphase I, homologs segregate towards opposite poles; the unpaired X chromosome, however, remains behind and attached to microtubules connected to separating poles before resolving to one side (Figure 1A, M I, arrowheads, Figure 1—video 1; Albertson and Thomson, 1993).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature and by the live imaging data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: In meiosis I, the unpaired X appears attached to both poles in contrast to the paired autosomes, each of which attaches to a single, opposite pole to enable segregation of homologs.
source: Thus in meiosis I, the unpaired X appears attached to both poles in contrast to the paired autosomes, each of which attaches to a single, opposite pole to enable segregation of homologs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that the X lags between separating poles while autosomes segregate.

claim: In the second division, sister chromatids of each chromosome segregate all away from one another to opposite poles.
source: In the second division, sister chromatids of each chromosome segregate all away from one another to opposite poles (Figure 1A,M II).
evidence: This statement is supported by the live imaging data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Paired X chromosomes in wild-type XX hermaphrodite spermatocytes do not lag during anaphase I.
source: First, though the unpaired X chromosome lags in wild-type XO males, paired X chromosomes in wild-type XX hermaphrodite spermatocytes did not.
evidence: This statement is based on live imaging data comparing males and hermaphrodites shown in Figure 1B.

claim: In hermaphrodite spermatocytes, an initial delay in the segregation of a chromosome was noticed in 5 out of 10 cases, but this slight lagging was not obvious at mid to late anaphase I.
source: Although we noticed an initial delay in the segregation of a chromosome in hermaphrodite spermatocytes (n = 5/10), this slight lagging was not obvious at mid to late anaphase I.
evidence: This statement is based on quantitative analysis of live imaging data.

claim: In over 80% of tra-2(e1094) XX male spindles, no lagging chromosomes were detected during meiosis I.
source: In over 80% (n = 43/53) of tra-2(e1094) XX male spindles we did not detect lagging chromosomes during meiosis I.
evidence: This statement is based on quantitative analysis of live imaging data.

claim: In about 20% of tra-2(e1094) spindles, lagging was detected to some extent, possibly due to improper pairing in prophase.
source: However, in about 20% of tra-2(e1094) spindles, we detected lagging to some extent, possibly due to improper pairing in prophase.
evidence: This statement is based on quantitative analysis of live imaging data and includes speculation about the cause.

claim: The majority of paired X chromosomes in male spermatocyte spindles do not lag in mid/late anaphase I.
source: Therefore, the majority of paired X chromosomes in male spermatocyte spindles do not lag in mid/late anaphase I, similar to paired sex chromosomes in hermaphrodite spermatocytes.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the tra-2(e1094) data.

claim: A mutation of him-8 results in lack of pairing of the X; thus, pairing, synapsis, and recombination of the X chromosomes do not occur.
source: A mutation of him-8 results in lack of pairing of the X; thus, pairing, synapsis, and recombination of the X chromosomes do not occur (Phillips et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Lagging chromosomes were observed in anaphase I in 70% of the analyzed him-8(e1489) spindles in hermaphrodite spermatocytes.
source: We observed lagging chromosomes in anaphase I in 70% (n = 14/20) of the analyzed him-8(e1489) spindles in hermaphrodite spermatocytes, presumably representing the two unpaired X chromosomes.
evidence: This statement is based on quantitative analysis of live imaging data.

claim: Anaphase I chromosome lagging is likely caused by an inability to undergo synapsis rather than by a somatic effect of the male sex.
source: This reveals that anaphase I chromosome lagging is likely caused by an inability to undergo synapsis rather than by a somatic effect of the male sex.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the him-8(e1489) data showing lagging in hermaphrodites.

claim: The zim-2(tm574) mutation prevents pairing of autosome V.
source: We further excluded that lagging is exclusive to the X chromosome by analyzing hermaphrodite and male spermatocytes with the zim-2(tm574) mutation, which prevents pairing of autosome V (Phillips and Dernburg, 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: At least one chromosome lagged in all spindles in zim-2(tm574) hermaphrodite (n = 10) and male spermatocytes (n = 5).
source: At least one chromosome lagged in all spindles in hermaphrodite (n = 10) and male spermatocytes (n = 5).
evidence: This statement is based on quantitative analysis of live imaging data.

claim: In triploid males with spermatocytes containing five unpaired autosomes, a massive fluorescent signal between segregating autosomes was detected that likely corresponds to the five unpaired autosomes in all spindles (n = 32).
source: Moreover, we created triploid males with spermatocytes containing five unpaired autosomes (Madl and Herman, 1979) and detected a massive fluorescent signal between segregating autosomes that we infer likely corresponds to the five unpaired autosomes in all spindles (n = 32).
evidence: This statement is based on quantitative analysis of live imaging data and includes inference about the identity of the lagging chromosomes.

claim: Lagging chromosomes during spermatocyte anaphase I are a consequence of the lack of pairing and synapsis of any chromosome during prophase I and are not specific to sex chromosomes.
source: Collectively, these results show that lagging chromosomes during spermatocyte anaphase I are indeed a consequence of the lack of pairing and synapsis of any chromosome during prophase I and are not specific to sex chromosomes.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined data from multiple mutants showing that any unpaired chromosome can lag.

claim: The lagging X chromosome changes shape during anaphase I.
source: During anaphase I, we observed that the lagging X changes shape (Figure 2A, upper panel).
evidence: This statement is based on live imaging data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The X chromosome was significantly stretched early in anaphase I with a shape coefficient of 1.4 that decreased to 1.0 as it rounded up in late anaphase I.
source: Indeed, the X chromosome was significantly stretched early in anaphase I with a shape coefficient of 1.4 that decreased to 1.0 as it rounded up in late anaphase I (Figure 2B).
evidence: This statement is based on quantitative analysis of 3D fluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The X chromosome is under tension from pulling forces as spindle poles separate, which is released as the lagging chromosome resolves to one side.
source: This suggests that the X is under tension from pulling forces as spindle poles separate, which is released as the lagging chromosome resolves to one side.
evidence: This is an inference based on the shape change data showing stretching and subsequent rounding of the X chromosome.

claim: Laser point-ablation to the bundle on one side of the X caused an immediate and continuous movement of the X towards the unablated side in 21 out of 26 cases.
source: Laser point-ablation to the bundle on one side of the X caused an immediate and continuous movement of the X towards the unablated side (n = 21/26, two examples shown; Figure 2C, Figure 2—video 1).
evidence: This statement is based on quantitative analysis of laser microsurgery experiments shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The velocity of the X chromosome movement after the laser cut was variable, similar to unperturbed spindles.
source: The velocity of the X chromosome movement after the cut was variable, similar to unperturbed spindles, which also displayed variability in the speed of X chromosome movement, ranging from 0.7 to 4.9 µm/min (mean = 2.2 µm/min, n = 40) and the onset of X chromosome movement relative to anaphase onset, ranging from 1.5 to 8.5 min (mean = 4.9 min, n = 55, data not shown).
evidence: This statement is based on quantitative analysis of laser microsurgery and live imaging data.

claim: After initiation of movement by the first cut, a second cut on the opposite side caused a rapid shift in the direction of segregation.
source: After initiation of movement by the first cut, the second cut on the opposite side caused a rapid shift in the direction of segregation, indicating microtubule connections are highly dynamic during anaphase I.
evidence: This statement is based on double-cut laser microsurgery experiments shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Microtubule connections are highly dynamic during anaphase I.
source: After initiation of movement by the first cut, the second cut on the opposite side caused a rapid shift in the direction of segregation, indicating microtubule connections are highly dynamic during anaphase I.
evidence: This is an inference based on the double-cut laser microsurgery experiments.

claim: Kinetochore microtubules exert a pulling force on chromosomes during anaphase.
source: Taken together, we conclude that kinetochore microtubules exert a pulling force on chromosomes during anaphase.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the shape change and laser microsurgery data.

claim: Tension from pulling forces is most obvious on the microtubules connected to the X chromosome.
source: This tension is most obvious on the microtubules connected to the X chromosome.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that the X chromosome shows the most dramatic shape changes and response to laser ablation.

claim: In oocyte meiosis, the localization of outer kinetochore proteins on chromosomes drops dramatically during anaphase I.
source: However, in oocyte meiosis the localization of outer kinetochore proteins on chromosomes drops dramatically during anaphase I, allowing central spindle components to largely drive chromosome movement (Dumont and Desai, 2012; Dumont et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The outer kinetochore proteins KNL-1, KNL-3 and NDC-80 are retained on the poleward sides of the rounded chromosomes in a cup-shaped pattern on autosomes and X chromosome during anaphase I in spermatocytes.
source: Strikingly, the outer kinetochore proteins, KNL-1 (Desai et al., 2003), KNL-3 (Cheeseman et al., 2004) and NDC-80 (Desai et al., 2003) are retained on the poleward sides of the rounded chromosomes in a cup-shaped pattern on autosomes and X chromosome during anaphase I (Figure 2E and Appendix 1—figure 1), in contrast to their rapid depletion during oocyte meiosis.
evidence: This statement is based on immunofluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 2E and Appendix 1—figure 1.

claim: Outer kinetochore retention suggests that chromosome-to-pole attachments are important to drive chromosome movement during sperm anaphase.
source: Outer kinetochore retention suggests that chromosome-to-pole attachments are important to drive chromosome movement during sperm anaphase.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that kinetochore proteins are retained during anaphase I in spermatocytes.

claim: Kinetochores bridge interactions between chromosomes and microtubules in spermatocytes.
source: Using super-resolution microscopy, we further found kinetochores bridge interactions between chromosomes and microtubules (Appendix 1—figure 1).
evidence: This statement is based on super-resolution microscopy data shown in Appendix 1—figure 1.

source: For metaphase I,~30–38% were kinetochore microtubules, which increased to ~45–53% for anaphase I (Table 1).

source: For metaphase I,~30–38% were kinetochore microtubules, which increased to ~45–53% for anaphase I (Table 1).

source: Interestingly, this percentage is much higher compared to early mitosis where only 2–4% of all microtubules attach to the kinetochore (Redemann et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement compares the current data to prior literature on mitotic spindles.

source: Similar to previous analysis of oocyte meiosis (Dumont et al., 2010; Laband et al., 2017; Muscat et al., 2015; Redemann et al., 2018), we recognized both a lateral and an end-on association of kinetochore microtubules to chromosomes (for details see Table 1).
evidence: This statement is based on analysis of electron tomography data and comparison to prior literature.

claim: Both types of association (lateral and end-on) were found for the autosomes and the unpaired X at all reconstructed meiotic stages.
source: We found both types of association for the autosomes and the unpaired X at all reconstructed meiotic stages.
evidence: This statement is based on quantitative analysis of electron tomography data across multiple stages.

claim: A complex pattern of both lateral and end-on associations is maintained throughout male meiotic progression.
source: This indicated to us that a complex pattern of both lateral and end-on associations is maintained throughout male meiotic progression.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observation that both types of associations are present at all stages.

claim: Microtubules directly connect the X to each centrosome throughout anaphase I.
source: We found that microtubules directly connect the X to each centrosome throughout anaphase I (Figures 5A–B and 4B–E, mid right panels, Appendix 1—figure 5A and B).
evidence: This statement is based on electron tomography data shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Microtubules with both end-on and lateral associations to X increased in length as X chromosome-to-pole distance increased until the X resolved to one side.
source: Further, microtubules with both end-on and lateral associations to X increased in length as X chromosome-to-pole distance increased until the X resolved to one side (Figure 5C–D).
evidence: This statement is based on quantitative analysis of electron tomography data shown in Figure 5C-D.

claim: Continuous microtubules connect the X chromosome to poles even as poles elongate during anaphase I.
source: Thus, continuous microtubules connect the X chromosome to poles even as poles elongate during anaphase I, consistent with the observation that outer kinetochore protein levels are retained on the X throughout spermatocyte divisions (Figure 2E, Appendix 1—figure 1).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the electron tomography data and consistent with the immunofluorescence data.

claim: X-associated microtubules were curved during late anaphase I.
source: We also observed that X-associated microtubules were curved during late anaphase I.
evidence: This statement is based on visual observation of electron tomography data.

claim: At metaphase I and anaphase I onset, the tortuosity ratio of X-connected kinetochore microtubules was one, indicating kinetochore microtubules were straight.
source: At metaphase I and anaphase I onset, the tortuosity ratio was one, indicating kinetochore microtubules were straight.
evidence: This statement is based on quantitative analysis of microtubule tortuosity from electron tomography data.

claim: At anaphase, X-connected microtubules exhibited higher tortuosity, indicating higher curvature.
source: However, at anaphase, X-connected microtubules exhibited higher tortuosity, indicating higher curvature (Figures Appendix 1—figures 6B and 5C-D).
evidence: This statement is based on quantitative analysis of microtubule tortuosity from electron tomography data.

claim: Laterally associated microtubules had a higher degree of tortuosity compared to end-on associated microtubules.
source: In addition, laterally associated microtubules had a higher degree of tortuosity compared to end-on associated microtubules.
evidence: This statement is based on quantitative analysis of microtubule tortuosity from electron tomography data.

claim: Other cellular forces, besides those generated by pulling forces, may be acting on microtubules connected to the lagging X during anaphase I.
source: This suggests that other cellular forces, besides those generated by pulling forces, may also be acting on microtubules connected to the lagging X during anaphase I.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation of increased microtubule curvature during anaphase.

claim: The ratio of total microtubule length on each side of X was about one in metaphase and early anaphase.
source: The ratio of total microtubule length and microtubule number were about one in metaphase and early anaphase, suggesting microtubules are present equally on both sides.
evidence: This statement is based on quantitative analysis of electron tomography data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: As anaphase progresses, the ratio of microtubule length and number on each side of X deviated from one, indicating less microtubules on one side.
source: As anaphase progresses, this ratio deviated from one, indicating less microtubules on one side that presumably enable the X to resolve to the opposing side.
evidence: This statement is based on quantitative analysis of electron tomography data shown in Figure 6B and D.

claim: An asymmetry in associated microtubules correlates with X chromosome resolution.
source: Thus, an asymmetry in associated microtubules correlates with X chromosome resolution, where attachments likely stochastically break as poles separate, allowing the X to resolve to the side with more associated microtubules.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the electron tomography and live imaging data showing asymmetry in microtubule numbers correlating with X chromosome movement.

claim: Attachments likely stochastically break as poles separate, allowing the X to resolve to the side with more associated microtubules.
source: Thus, an asymmetry in associated microtubules correlates with X chromosome resolution, where attachments likely stochastically break as poles separate, allowing the X to resolve to the side with more associated microtubules.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the data showing asymmetry in microtubule numbers.

claim: A hallmark of anaphase progression in C. elegans embryonic mitosis and oocyte meiosis is a structure of overlapping spindle midzone microtubules that forms between separating chromosomes known as the central spindle.
source: A hallmark of anaphase progression in C. elegans embryonic mitosis and oocyte meiosis is a structure of overlapping spindle midzone microtubules that forms between separating chromosomes known as the central spindle (Yu et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Only a weak microtubule signal was detected in early anaphase I between segregating chromosomes in tra-2(e1094) XX males by live imaging.
source: By live imaging, we detected only a weak microtubule signal in early anaphase I between segregating chromosomes (Appendix 1—figure 7A).
evidence: This statement is based on live imaging data shown in Appendix 1—figure 7A.

claim: tra-2(e1094) males without a lagging chromosome exhibited a faster spindle elongation rate and a longer final pole-to-pole distance compared to wild-type males that have a lagging X.
source: Interestingly, tra-2(e1094) males without a lagging chromosome exhibited a faster spindle elongation rate and a longer final pole-to-pole distance compared to wild-type males that have a lagging X (Appendix 1—figure 7A, B and Figure 1B).
evidence: This statement is based on quantitative analysis of live imaging data comparing tra-2(e1094) males to wild-type males.

claim: About 160 microtubules were detected in the anaphase I spindle midzone of tra-2(e1094) males by electron tomography.
source: By electron tomography, we detected about 160 microtubules in the anaphase I spindle midzone of tra-2(e1094) males (Appendix 1—figure 7C; Appendix 1—figure 7—video 1).
evidence: This statement is based on quantitative analysis of electron tomography data shown in Appendix 1—figure 7C.

claim: Microtubules in the midzone of tra-2(e1094) males did not show an interdigitated pattern characteristic of C. elegans mitotic or oocyte meiotic spindle midzones.
source: These microtubules, however, did not show an interdigitated pattern characteristic of C. elegans mitotic or oocyte meiotic spindle midzones (Yu et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is based on analysis of electron tomography data and comparison to prior literature.

claim: Even in the absence of a lagging chromosome, male meiotic spindles do not form a typical spindle midzone of overlapping microtubules.
source: Thus, even in the absence of a lagging chromosome, male meiotic spindles do not form a typical spindle midzone of overlapping microtubules.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the electron tomography data from tra-2(e1094) males.

claim: Central spindle specifiers did not localize within the midzone during mid to late sperm meiotic anaphase I in both the presence (him-8(e1489)) or absence (tra-2(e1094)) of a lagging X chromosome.
source: Further, central spindle specifiers that localize in the spindle midzone in oocyte meiosis and mitosis did not localize within the midzone during mid to late sperm meiotic anaphase I in both the presence (him-8(e1489)) or absence (tra-2(e1094)) of a lagging X chromosome (Appendix 1—figure 8A).
evidence: This statement is based on immunofluorescence microscopy data shown in Appendix 1—figure 8A.

claim: Aurora BAIR-2 associated with separating autosomes or the lagging X during anaphase I in spermatocytes.
source: First, Aurora BAIR-2, a component of the chromosomal passenger complex (Davies et al., 2014; de Carvalho et al., 2008; Dumont et al., 2010; Maton et al., 2015; Schumacher et al., 1998; Severson et al., 2000), associated with separating autosomes or the lagging X during anaphase I.
evidence: This statement is based on immunofluorescence microscopy data and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: CLASPCLS-2 localized to the inside face of separating chromosomes and remained chromosome-associated during anaphase I in spermatocytes.
source: CLASPCLS-2, a microtubule stabilizer (Dumont et al., 2010; Maton et al., 2015; Nahaboo et al., 2015), localized to the inside face of separating chromosomes and remained chromosome-associated during anaphase I.
evidence: This statement is based on immunofluorescence microscopy data and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: MKLP1ZEN-4 localized between separating chromosomes at very early anaphase, then to the cell membrane in a ring-like structure likely on the ingressing furrow at mid-anaphase in spermatocytes.
source: A centralspindlin component, MKLP1ZEN-4, localized between separating chromosomes at very early anaphase, then to the cell membrane in a ring-like structure likely on the ingressing furrow at mid-anaphase (Powers et al., 1998; Raich et al., 1998).
evidence: This statement is based on immunofluorescence microscopy data and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: PRC1SPD-1 initially briefly localized between segregating autosomes and around the X chromosome in very early anaphase I, but rapidly disappeared as anaphase I progressed in males and hermaphrodite spermatocytes.
source: Similarly, using live-imaging, PRC1SPD-1 (Mullen and Wignall, 2017; Nahaboo et al., 2015; Verbrugghe and White, 2004), a known microtubule bundling factor, initially briefly localized between segregating autosomes and around the X chromosome in very early anaphase I, but rapidly disappeared as anaphase I progressed in males and hermaphrodite spermatocytes (Appendix 1—figure 8B).
evidence: This statement is based on live imaging data shown in Appendix 1—figure 8B and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Spindle elongation, the segregation of autosomes, and the resolution of the X continued even without a detectable signal of PRC1SPD-1 in between chromosomes.
source: Thus, spindle elongation, the segregation of autosomes, and the resolution of the X continued even without a detectable signal of PRC1SPD-1 in between chromosomes.
evidence: This is an observation based on the live imaging data showing chromosome movement continues after PRC1SPD-1 disappears.

claim: Male meiotic spindles, in the presence or absence of a lagging X, do not form a 'canonical' midzone structure during mid-to-late anaphase I.
source: Overall, these results suggest that male meiotic spindles, in the presence or absence of a lagging X, do not form a 'canonical' midzone structure during mid-to-late anaphase I.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined electron tomography and immunofluorescence data.

claim: In meiosis I, the pole-to-pole distance increased from 4.1 ± 0.3 µm to 8.0 ± 0.6 µm (mean ± SD; n = 31).
source: In meiosis I (Figure 7A–B; Figure 7—video 1), the pole-to-pole distance increased from 4.1 ± 0.3 µm to 8.0 ± 0.6 µm (mean ± SD; n = 31) with an elongation speed of 1.29 ± 0.36 µm/min (Figure 7E).
evidence: This statement is based on quantitative analysis of live imaging data shown in Figure 7.

claim: The pole-to-pole elongation speed in meiosis I is 1.29 ± 0.36 µm/min.
source: In meiosis I (Figure 7A–B; Figure 7—video 1), the pole-to-pole distance increased from 4.1 ± 0.3 µm to 8.0 ± 0.6 µm (mean ± SD; n = 31) with an elongation speed of 1.29 ± 0.36 µm/min (Figure 7E).
evidence: This statement is based on quantitative analysis of live imaging data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: The pole-to-pole elongation speed in spermatocyte meiosis I is significantly higher compared to 0.6-0.8 µm/min reported for both female meiotic divisions.
source: This speed is significantly higher compared to 0.6–0.8 µm/min reported for both female meiotic divisions (McNally et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement compares the current data to prior literature on oocyte meiosis.

claim: Pole-to-autosome distance decreased by half in meiosis I, from 1.6 ± 0.3 µm to 0.8 ± 0.3 µm with a speed of 0.39 ± 0.27 µm/min.
source: We also found a simultaneous anaphase A-type movement in spermatocytes with pole-to-autosome distance decreased by half, from 1.6 ± 0.3 µm to 0.8 ± 0.3 µm and a speed of 0.39 ± 0.27 µm/min (Table 2).
evidence: This statement is based on quantitative analysis of live imaging data shown in Table 2.

claim: The autosome-to-autosome distance increased from 0.9 ± 0.2 µm to 6.5 ± 0.4 µm in meiosis I.
source: In addition, the autosome-to-autosome distance increased from 0.9 ± 0.2 µm to 6.5 ± 0.4 µm (mean ± SD; n = 31).
evidence: This statement is based on quantitative analysis of live imaging data.

claim: From the 5 µm increase in autosome-to-autosome distance, anaphase B provides about 4 µm (~80%) of separation, whereas anaphase A provides only 1 µm (~20%).
source: Roughly, from this 5 µm increase in autosome-to-autosome distance, anaphase B provides about 4 µm (~80%) of separation, whereas anaphase A provides only 1 µm (~20%).
evidence: This is a calculation based on the measured distances showing the relative contributions of anaphase A and B.

claim: Chromosome dynamics in meiosis II also exhibited anaphase A and anaphase B-type movements.
source: Chromosome dynamics in meiosis II also exhibited anaphase A and anaphase B-type movements (Figure 7C–D and F; Figure 7—video 2; Table 2).
evidence: This statement is based on quantitative analysis of live imaging data shown in Figure 7 and Table 2.

claim: Spermatocyte meiotic spindles in C. elegans exhibit both anaphase A and B-type movements.
source: Taken together, spermatocyte meiotic spindles in C. elegans exhibit both anaphase A and B-type movements.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the live imaging data showing both types of movement.

claim: Spermatocyte meiotic spindles are distinct from mitosis in the early C. elegans embryo, which utilizes only anaphase B mechanisms.
source: This is distinct from mitosis in the early C. elegans embryo, which utilizes only anaphase B mechanisms (Oegema et al., 2001), or oocyte meiosis, which uses acentrosomal mechanisms (Dumont et al., 2010; McNally et al., 2016; Muscat et al., 2015; Redemann et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement compares the current findings to prior literature on embryonic mitosis.

claim: Spermatocyte meiotic spindles are distinct from oocyte meiosis, which uses acentrosomal mechanisms.
source: This is distinct from mitosis in the early C. elegans embryo, which utilizes only anaphase B mechanisms (Oegema et al., 2001), or oocyte meiosis, which uses acentrosomal mechanisms (Dumont et al., 2010; McNally et al., 2016; Muscat et al., 2015; Redemann et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement compares the current findings to prior literature on oocyte meiosis.

claim: Similar to grasshopper spermatocytes, anaphase A and B movement occurs simultaneously in C. elegans spermatocytes.
source: Similar to grasshopper spermatocytes (Ris, 1949), anaphase A and B movement occurs simultaneously, with anaphase A contributing approximately one fifth to the overall chromosome displacement.
evidence: This statement compares the current findings to prior literature on grasshopper spermatocytes.

claim: Anaphase A contributes approximately one fifth to the overall chromosome displacement in C. elegans spermatocytes.
source: Similar to grasshopper spermatocytes (Ris, 1949), anaphase A and B movement occurs simultaneously, with anaphase A contributing approximately one fifth to the overall chromosome displacement.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the measured distances showing the relative contribution of anaphase A.

claim: A well-described mechanism for anaphase A is microtubule shortening.
source: A well-described mechanism for anaphase A (i.e. a decrease in chromosome-to-pole length) is microtubule shortening (Asbury, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: In the earliest metaphase I data set, end-on kinetochore microtubules associated to autosomes were slightly longer (0.79 ± 0.3 µm; n = 153) than all other data sets.
source: We set the metaphase I (data set Metaphase no. 1) as the earliest, since end-on kinetochore microtubules associated to autosomes were slightly longer than all other data sets (0.79 ± 0.3 µm; n = 153; Figure 7G).
evidence: This statement is based on quantitative analysis of electron tomography data shown in Figure 7G.

claim: In both other metaphase data sets, the length of end-on associated microtubules was 0.62 and 0.68 µm.
source: In both other metaphase data sets, the length of end-on associated microtubules was 0.62 and 0.68 µm.
evidence: This statement is based on quantitative analysis of electron tomography data.

claim: As anaphase I progressed and the autosome-to-pole distance decreased, end-on kinetochore microtubules did not significantly shorten, remaining at 0.59-0.65 µm.
source: Unexpectedly, as anaphase I progressed and the autosome-to-pole distance decreased, we observed that end-on kinetochore microtubules did not significantly shorten, remaining at 0.59–0.65 µm (Appendix 1—figure 9A and Appendix 1—figure 5E).
evidence: This statement is based on quantitative analysis of electron tomography data shown in Appendix 1—figure 9A.

claim: The length of laterally associated microtubules increased from 1.28 µm in metaphase to 1.44 µm in anaphase.
source: Interestingly, the length of laterally associated microtubules did increase from 1.28 µm in metaphase to 1.44 µm in anaphase (Figure 7H, Appendix 1—figures 9B and 5F).
evidence: This statement is based on quantitative analysis of electron tomography data shown in Figure 7H.

claim: Shortening of kinetochore microtubules does not fully account for the anaphase A observed by light microscopy in spermatocytes.
source: Thus, unlike in other systems (Asbury, 2017), our tomographic analysis suggests that shortening of kinetochore microtubules does not fully account for the anaphase A observed by light microscopy.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the electron tomography data showing constant microtubule lengths.

claim: Changes in the shape of chromosomes, centrosomes, and the association angles of kinetochore microtubules with autosomes induced by tension released at the metaphase to anaphase transition may contribute to the decrease in chromosome-to-centrosome distance.
source: To account for anaphase A in spermatocyte meiosis, we hypothesized that changes in the shape of chromosomes, centrosomes, and the association angles of kinetochore microtubules with autosomes induced by tension released at the metaphase to anaphase transition (Dumont and Mitchison, 2009; Gardner et al., 2005) may contribute to the decrease in chromosome-to-centrosome distance.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed to explain the anaphase A movement observed without microtubule shortening.

claim: The autosomes of the first metaphase data set were the least stretched (0.52 ± 0.03 µm).
source: The autosomes of the first metaphase data set were the least stretched (0.52 ± 0.03 µm), consistent that the chromosomes in this data set were not yet under full tension.
evidence: This statement is based on quantitative analysis of chromosome shape from electron tomography data.

claim: Chromosomes in metaphase data set no. two were most stretched (0.73 ± 0.12 µm).
source: Chromosomes in metaphase data set no. two were most stretched (0.73 ± 0.12 µm).
evidence: This statement is based on quantitative analysis of chromosome shape from electron tomography data.

claim: As chromosomes separated, autosomes rounded up to a value of 0.56 µm in anaphase data sets no. four and no. 7.
source: As chromosomes separated, autosomes rounded up to a value of 0.56 µm in anaphase data sets no. four and no. 7 (Figure 8B, Appendix 1—figure 5G).
evidence: This statement is based on quantitative analysis of chromosome shape from electron tomography data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The rounding up of autosomes during anaphase is about 23% less compared to metaphase no. 2.
source: This is about 23% less compared to metaphase no. 2, thereby moving chromosome centers closer to the poles.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the measured chromosome stretch values.

claim: The release during anaphase of chromosome stretch induced by metaphase alignment accounts for a portion of anaphase A pole-chromosome shortening.
source: Thus, the release during anaphase of chromosome stretch induced by metaphase alignment accounts for a portion of anaphase A pole-chromosome shortening.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the chromosome shape analysis.

claim: The distance of the plus-end of the kinetochore microtubules to the closest centriole significantly shortened when comparing metaphase data sets (0.99-1.14 µm) to the anaphase data sets (0.78-0.95 µm).
source: This distance significantly shortened when comparing metaphase data sets (0.99–1.14 µm) to the anaphase data sets (0.78–0.95 µm; Figure 8D, Appendix 1—figure 5H), resulting in autosomes being 0.2 µm or 20% closer to centrioles.
evidence: This statement is based on quantitative analysis of electron tomography data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Changes in centrosome size and shape result in autosomes being 0.2 µm or 20% closer to centrioles.
source: This distance significantly shortened when comparing metaphase data sets (0.99–1.14 µm) to the anaphase data sets (0.78–0.95 µm; Figure 8D, Appendix 1—figure 5H), resulting in autosomes being 0.2 µm or 20% closer to centrioles.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the measured distances.

claim: The angle between kinetochore microtubule plus-ends and the centrosome-chromosome axis in the metaphase data sets was 37°-41°.
source: The angle in the metaphase data sets was 37°- 41°.
evidence: This statement is based on quantitative analysis of electron tomography data.

claim: As autosomes rounded up during anaphase, the attachment angle in the anaphase data sets increased to 46°-59°.
source: As autosomes rounded up during anaphase, the attachment angle in the anaphase data sets increased to 46°- 59°, bringing chromosomes closer to poles (Figure 8F, Appendix 1—figure 5I).
evidence: This statement is based on quantitative analysis of electron tomography data shown in Figure 8F.

claim: The increase in the attachment angle contributes about 0.17 µm or 17% shortening in chromosome-to-pole distance.
source: Simple trigonometric calculations with a constant microtubule length of 0.63 µm found this increase in the attachment angle contributes about 0.17 µm or 17% shortening in chromosome-to-pole distance.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the measured angles and microtubule lengths.

claim: Three factors contribute to pole-chromosome shortening during anaphase: 1) a loss of chromosome stretch during anaphase, which shortens the chromosome by about 0.34 µm; 2) changes in centrosome size and shape that contributes about 0.2 µm; and 3) the opening of the attachment angle that accounts for 0.17 µm.
source: In sum, we identify three factors that contribute to pole-chromosomes shortening during anaphase: 1) a loss of chromosome stretch during anaphase, which shortens the chromosome by about 0.34 µm; 2) changes in centrosome size and shape that contributes about 0.2 µm; and 3) the opening of the attachment angle that accounts for 0.17 µm.
evidence: This is a summary of the three mechanisms identified through quantitative analysis of electron tomography data.

claim: These three factors comprise approximately 70% of the total approximately 1 µm chromosome-to-pole distance shortening observed in spermatocyte meiosis.
source: These factors comprise ~70% of the total ~1 µm chromosome-to-pole distance shortening observed in spermatocyte meiosis, though this may be underestimated due to limitations in the tomographic reconstruction from serial semi-thick sections.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the sum of the three identified mechanisms.

claim: The contribution of the three factors to anaphase A may be underestimated due to limitations in the tomographic reconstruction from serial semi-thick sections.
source: These factors comprise ~70% of the total ~1 µm chromosome-to-pole distance shortening observed in spermatocyte meiosis, though this may be underestimated due to limitations in the tomographic reconstruction from serial semi-thick sections.
evidence: This is a caveat about potential limitations of the electron tomography method.

claim: The ultrastructure analysis revealed previously unknown, alternative mechanisms that contribute to anaphase-A movement.
source: Overall, our ultrastructure analysis revealed previously unknown, alternative mechanisms that contribute to anaphase-A movement.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the novelty of the findings.

claim: Prior to this work, only a handful of studies addressed spermatocyte spindle dynamics during male meiosis.
source: Prior to this work, only a handful of studies addressed spermatocyte spindle dynamics during male meiosis (Fegaras and Forer, 2018; Felt et al., 2017; Golding and Paliulis, 2011; LaFountain et al., 2011; LaFountain et al., 2012; Nicklas and Kubai, 1985; Nicklas et al., 2001; Zhang and Nicklas, 1995).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The large-scale tomographic reconstruction combined with live imaging and immunostaining in C. elegans provides an in-depth characterization of the molecular architecture and dynamics of the male meiotic spindle.
source: Our large-scale tomographic reconstruction combined with live imaging and immunostaining in C. elegans now provides an in-depth characterization of the molecular architecture and dynamics of the male meiotic spindle.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the contribution of the study.

claim: The absence of a pairing partner and/or the inability to pair induces any chromosome to lag in C. elegans spermatocytes.
source: We determined new molecular features of chromosome lagging and resolution in C. elegans. We show the absence of a pairing partner and/or the inability to pair induces any chromosome to lag.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data from multiple mutants showing that any unpaired chromosome can lag.

claim: Microtubule 'bridges' to lagging chromosomes consist of continuous microtubules that attach to each side and lengthen during anaphase I.
source: Furthermore, microtubule 'bridges' to lagging chromosomes consist of continuous microtubules that attach to each side and lengthen during anaphase I.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the electron tomography data showing continuous microtubules connecting the X to both poles.

claim: Both end-on and laterally-associated microtubules were detected on the lagging X.
source: Moreover, we detected both end-on and laterally-associated microtubules on the lagging X.
evidence: This statement is based on quantitative analysis of electron tomography data.

claim: The lagging X has both end-on and lateral microtubule associations, which is distinct from embryonic mitosis where the vast majority of microtubules make end-on attachments to rod-like chromosomes.
source: This is distinct from embryonic mitosis, where the vast majority of microtubules make end-on attachments to rod-like chromosomes (O'Toole et al., 2003; Redemann et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement compares the current findings to prior literature on embryonic mitosis.

claim: Kinetochore microtubules may grow at their plus ends as poles move apart to maintain kinetochore microtubule association to the X.
source: Possibly, kinetochore microtubules grow at their plus ends as poles move apart. Microtubule growth at a similar rate to spindle elongation would maintain kinetochore microtubule association to the X.
evidence: This is speculation about a possible mechanism for microtubule lengthening.

claim: The growth rate of kinetochore microtubules could exceed the rate of spindle elongation, thus allowing minus-end directed interactions of motor proteins such as dynein.
source: Alternatively, the growth rate of kinetochore microtubules could exceed the rate of spindle elongation, thus allowing minus-end directed interactions of motor proteins such as dynein (Reck-Peterson et al., 2018; Schmidt et al., 2005; Schmidt et al., 2017).
evidence: This is speculation about an alternative mechanism for microtubule lengthening, supported by citations to prior literature on dynein.

claim: An imbalance of pulling forces may result stochastically from continuous attachment and detachment of kinetochore microtubules in a 'tug-of-war' model.
source: Our analyses support that an imbalance of pulling forces may result stochastically from continuous attachment and detachment of kinetochore microtubules. In such a 'tug-of-war' model, the side that maintains more connections wins (Appendix 1—figure 10A).
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the data showing asymmetry in microtubule numbers correlating with X chromosome resolution.

claim: A similar 'tug-of-war' mechanism has been suggested during chromosomal oscillations at mitotic prometaphase and metaphase.
source: A similar mechanism has also been suggested during chromosomal oscillations at mitotic prometaphase and metaphase (Ault et al., 1991; Skibbens et al., 1993; Soppina et al., 2009) with chromokinesins and dynein as possible candidates for switching the direction of the oscillations (Sutradhar and Paul, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature on chromosome oscillations.

claim: Microtubule breakage was suggested to initiate the segregation of merotelically attached mammalian kinetochores.
source: As for the initiation of segregation, an analogous situation is the segregation of merotelically attached mammalian kinetochores, where microtubule breakage was suggested to initiate the segregation of lagging mitotic chromosomes (Cimini et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Many species have evolved distinct spindle structures and segregation strategies to resolve lagging of sex or unequal numbers of chromosomes.
source: Importantly, many species have evolved distinct spindle structures and segregation strategies to resolve lagging of sex or unequal numbers of chromosomes (Fabig et al., 2016; Shakes et al., 2011; Winter et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Segregation in cells with aneuploidy and chromosomal abnormalities are potential drivers of infertility.
source: Segregation in cells with aneuploidy and chromosomal abnormalities are potential drivers of infertility (Barri et al., 2005; García-Mengual et al., 2019; Hassold and Hunt, 2001; Ioannou and Tempest, 2015) and cancer progression (Bolhaqueiro et al., 2019; Chunduri and Storchová, 2019; Ly et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Segregation in cells with aneuploidy and chromosomal abnormalities are potential drivers of cancer progression.
source: Segregation in cells with aneuploidy and chromosomal abnormalities are potential drivers of infertility (Barri et al., 2005; García-Mengual et al., 2019; Hassold and Hunt, 2001; Ioannou and Tempest, 2015) and cancer progression (Bolhaqueiro et al., 2019; Chunduri and Storchová, 2019; Ly et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The studies can impact the understanding of partition mechanisms in other systems that segregate both paired and lagging chromosomes to efficiently and reliably generate cells with correct ploidy.
source: Thus, our studies can impact the understanding of partition mechanisms in other systems that segregate both paired and lagging chromosomes to efficiently and reliably generate cells with correct ploidy (Fabig et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a statement about the potential broader impact of the findings.

claim: The single-microtubule resolution of electron tomography unexpectedly revealed the lengths of autosomal end-on kinetochore microtubules are largely constant during sperm anaphase.
source: The single-microtubule resolution of electron tomography unexpectedly revealed the lengths of autosomal end-on kinetochore microtubules are largely constant during sperm anaphase.
evidence: This statement is based on quantitative analysis of electron tomography data.

claim: The finding that kinetochore microtubule lengths are constant is in contrast to the kinetochore microtubule shortening typically associated with anaphase A observed by light microscopy in many systems.
source: This is in contrast to the kinetochore microtubule shortening typically associated with anaphase A observed by light microscopy in many systems (Asbury, 2017).
evidence: This statement compares the current findings to prior literature on anaphase A mechanisms.

claim: Methods were developed to use ultrastructural data to identify three contributors to spermatocyte anaphase A.
source: Further, we developed methods to use ultrastructural data to identify three contributors to spermatocyte anaphase A (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a statement about the methodological contribution of the study.

claim: Autosomes stretched at metaphase relax from tension released by separase-mediated cleavage of cohesins at anaphase, resulting in chromosome shape change.
source: First, autosomes stretched at metaphase relax from tension released by separase-mediated cleavage of cohesins at anaphase (Severson and Meyer, 2014), resulting in chromosome shape change.
evidence: This statement is based on the chromosome shape analysis and supported by a citation to prior literature on cohesin cleavage.

claim: Spindle poles decrease in size and change shape as centrioles split, which shortens distance between microtubule plus-ends and centrioles.
source: Second, spindle poles decrease in size and change shape as centrioles split, which also shortens distance between microtubule plus-ends and centrioles.
evidence: This statement is based on quantitative analysis of electron tomography data.

claim: The ends of microtubules on chromosomes shift from a central to more peripheral position during anaphase, decreasing the microtubule-to-pole distance.
source: Third, the ends of microtubules on chromosomes shift from a central to more peripheral position during anaphase, decreasing the microtubule-to-pole distance.
evidence: This statement is based on quantitative analysis of microtubule attachment angles from electron tomography data.

claim: All three factors change the relative position of centrosomes, autosomes and kinetochore microtubules to one another independent of kinetochore microtubule shortening.
source: All three factors change the relative position of centrosomes, autosomes and kinetochore microtubules to one another independent of kinetochore microtubule shortening.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the three mechanisms identified.

claim: Microtubules can shorten during anaphase I, as observed when the X resolves to one side.
source: Microtubules can shorten during anaphase I, as observed when the X resolves to one side; thus, a shortening of a subset of microtubules that is difficult to detect by current methods may also contribute to a small portion of anaphase A movement.
evidence: This is an observation based on the electron tomography data showing shorter microtubules on one side of the X when it resolves.

claim: A shortening of a subset of microtubules that is difficult to detect by current methods may contribute to a small portion of anaphase A movement.
source: Microtubules can shorten during anaphase I, as observed when the X resolves to one side; thus, a shortening of a subset of microtubules that is difficult to detect by current methods may also contribute to a small portion of anaphase A movement.
evidence: This is speculation about a potential additional mechanism that may be difficult to detect.

claim: The proposed new mechanisms can now be considered when analyzing anaphase A movement in other systems.
source: Nonetheless, our proposed new mechanisms can now be considered when analyzing anaphase A movement in other systems (Appendix 1—figure 10B).
evidence: This is a statement about the potential broader impact of the findings.

claim: Important differences exist in the molecular composition of meiotic spindles in spermatocytes compared to those in oocyte meiosis and embryonic mitosis in C. elegans.
source: In C. elegans, we found important differences in the molecular composition of meiotic spindles in spermatocytes compared to those in oocyte meiosis and embryonic mitosis.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the findings comparing spermatocyte spindles to other cell types.

claim: Outer kinetochore proteins are retained and microtubules remain associated to chromosomes between meiotic divisions in spermatocytes.
source: First, outer kinetochore proteins are retained and microtubules remain associated to chromosomes between meiotic divisions in sharp contrast to oocyte meiotic anaphase, where kinetochore levels diminish dramatically and microtubules disassemble during anaphase I progression (Dumont et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is based on immunofluorescence and electron tomography data and comparison to prior literature on oocyte meiosis.

claim: Autosome-associated kinetochore microtubules are continuous and directly attached to poles in spermatocytes.
source: Second, autosome-associated kinetochore microtubules are continuous and directly attached to poles, in contrast to embryonic mitosis, where chromosome-connected microtubules end in the spindle matrix and make indirect contact with microtubules attached to poles (Redemann et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is based on electron tomography data and comparison to prior literature on embryonic mitosis.

claim: The direct kinetochore-to-pole connection in spermatocytes is related to the small size of spermatocytes, in contrast to the relatively large one-cell embryo.
source: We speculate that the direct kinetochore-to-pole connection in spermatocytes is related to the small size of spermatocytes, in contrast to the relatively large one-cell embryo (Redemann et al., 2017).
evidence: This is speculation about the reason for the observed difference in microtubule organization.

claim: Sperm-specific differences exist in central spindle architecture during anaphase I that may impact the lagging and resolution of the X chromosome.
source: Third, we find sperm-specific differences in central spindle architecture during anaphase I that also may impact the lagging and resolution of the X chromosome.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the findings on central spindle organization.

claim: When the X lags, microtubule bridges connected to X dominate the spindle midzone.
source: When the X lags, microtubule bridges connected to X dominate the spindle midzone. (Figures 1A and 4).
evidence: This statement is based on live imaging and electron tomography data.

claim: With no lagging chromosome in meiosis I in tra-2(e1090) mutant males, few microtubules are found between the separated chromosomes and they lack the classical overlapping structure thought to push chromosomes apart.
source: With no lagging chromosome in meiosis I in tra-2(e1090) mutant males, few microtubules are found between the separated chromosomes (Figure 1B and Appendix 1—figure 7) and they lack the classical overlapping structure thought to push chromosomes apart, as observed in either acentrosomal oocyte meiosis (Dumont et al., 2010; Laband et al., 2017; Redemann et al., 2018; Yu et al., 2019) or centrosomal embryonic mitosis (Nahaboo et al., 2015; Yu et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is based on electron tomography data from tra-2(e1090) males and comparison to prior literature.

claim: Central spindle specifiers have sperm-specific localization patterns at mid-late anaphase I instead of residing strongly within the spindle midzone.
source: Furthermore, central spindle specifiers have sperm-specific localization patterns at mid-late anaphase I instead of residing strongly within the spindle midzone (Davies et al., 2014; de Carvalho et al., 2008; Dumont et al., 2010; Maton et al., 2015; Schumacher et al., 1998; Severson et al., 2000).
evidence: This statement is based on immunofluorescence data and comparison to prior literature.

claim: Aurora B KinaseAIR-2 and CLASPCLS-2 stay associated with spermatocyte chromosomes during anaphase I.
source: Aurora B KinaseAIR-2 and CLASPCLS-2 stay associated with spermatocyte chromosomes (Appendix 1—figure 8A).
evidence: This statement is based on immunofluorescence microscopy data.

claim: MKLP1ZEN-4 localizes at the ingressing furrow during spermatocyte anaphase I.
source: Likewise, MKLP1ZEN-4, a centralspindlin component (Powers et al., 1998; Raich et al., 1998), localizes at the ingressing furrow.
evidence: This statement is based on immunofluorescence microscopy data and supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: PRC1SPD-1 is transiently present in very early anaphase but becomes undetectable during spermatocyte anaphase I.
source: PRC1SPD-1, a microtubule bundling protein (Verbrugghe and White, 2004), while transiently present in very early anaphase becomes undetectable (Appendix 1—figure 8B).
evidence: This statement is based on live imaging data and supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: C. elegans spermatocyte meiosis forms an alternate spindle midzone structure compared with mitosis or oocyte meiosis.
source: Thus, our results support that C. elegans spermatocyte meiosis forms an alternate spindle midzone structure compared with mitosis or oocyte meiosis.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined electron tomography and immunofluorescence data.

claim: The alternate midzone organization may have evolved to aid lagging chromosome resolution.
source: We speculate this may have evolved to aid lagging chromosome resolution, and it will be interesting to analyze meiotic spindle midzones in other systems with lagging sex chromosomes (Fabig et al., 2016).
evidence: This is speculation about the evolutionary significance of the observed midzone organization.

claim: The alternate midzone organization may stem from mechanisms that regulate cytokinesis to specify intracellular bridges that maintain the germline syncytium.
source: Alternatively, this midzone organization may stem from mechanisms that regulate cytokinesis to specify intracellular bridges that maintain the germline syncytium (Lee et al., 2018; Zhou et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an alternative speculation about the reason for the observed midzone organization, supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The approach combining quantification of 3D ultrastructure of staged spindles with live imaging and immunostaining in males lays the groundwork for further detailed studies on chromosome segregation.
source: In toto, our approach combining quantification of 3D ultrastructure of staged spindles with live imaging and immunostaining in males to identify sperm-specific features of meiosis lays the groundwork for further detailed studies on chromosome segregation and provides the necessary analytical tools for analyses on spindles in a broad range of different contexts.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the methodological contribution of the study.

claim: The approach provides the necessary analytical tools for analyses on spindles in a broad range of different contexts.
source: In toto, our approach combining quantification of 3D ultrastructure of staged spindles with live imaging and immunostaining in males to identify sperm-specific features of meiosis lays the groundwork for further detailed studies on chromosome segregation and provides the necessary analytical tools for analyses on spindles in a broad range of different contexts.
evidence: This is a statement about the potential broader impact of the methodological approach.
